https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.title: Roc Sandford fears for his children Blue and Lazer in HS2 tunnel protest
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/transport/ar.text:
An island laird has said that he fears for the lives of his son and daughter who are burrowed deep in a protest camp tunnel 500 miles away.
Speaking from his home on the Hebridean island of Gometra, Roc Sandford, an environmental activist, criticised health and safety chiefs.
Sandford said he had lodged a complaint with the Health and Safety Executive (HSE) for failing to halt eviction tactics he claims have put the lives at risk of his daughter Blue, son Lazer, and other protesters.
Blue, 18, and Lazer, 20, are in a 100ft-long tunnel secretly constructed under Euston Square Gardens in London by activists protesting against HS2’s high-speed rail development plan.
As safety fears grow for the small band of eco warriors who have witnessed five soil collapses in the tunnel as eviction teams worked on gaining access, the father urged HSE to intervene before someone is hurt.
The protesters have been in the tunnel since Wednesday and are considering legal action against HSE.
Sandford said: “It is clear that a dangerous situation is rapidly evolving which is within HSE’s statutory obligations to address with utmost urgency.
“This is an emergency. HSE’s current response is totally inadequate. Heads will roll at HSE on this, ideally at the top, they need to get in there before someone gets seriously hurt. This is not a time to get bureaucratic and play for time, they need to get down to Euston and do their job, which is to listen to what the protesters are saying and address the life-threatening risks they are being subjected to at the hands of HS2 and NET (National Eviction Team).”
Reiterating allegations made by the protesters in video footage, and calls for help from the depths of the tunnel, Sandford claims the eviction team has put lives at risk by denying activists the right to monitor oxygen levels in the depths of the tunnel and allowing water to flood in. He added: “My son Lazer was injured by a tree root dropped on him from nine feet up. This is putting lives at risk. I am not a lawyer but my understanding is that the actions of NET are clearly unlawful.”
Sandford is a member of Extinction Rebellion and has attended many climate protests. Now his children are following in his footsteps, although he says he is not as brave as them.
“They have completely outclassed me in their protests which proves it isn’t coming from me,” he said. “I am always begging them to be careful and I sometimes feel like I am going to collapse with fear but I am also so proud of what they are achieving.” He added: “We’re putting children in danger by using petrol, diesel, gas. This puts carbon dioxide into the atmosphere, which makes it heat up like a sauna, which causes food shortages, floods, burning forests and wars. It’s not a video game or a disaster movie, it’s real and it’s happening now all over the world and soon it will be happening to us.
“Top climate scientists are saying governments like ours are risking killing almost all our children. It’s as simple as that. My children have burrowed deep under Euston with their friends to protest HS2. They are being besieged down there.
“It’s so scary and I have been going though a really dark and miserable place knowing I could lose them. They are so brave to do this but they shouldn’t have to carry this responsibility.”
Greg Smith, MP for Buckingham, said: “I am concerned for the safety of all involved in these protest tunnels and have raised my concerns about the use of the HS2 National Eviction Team for this with the minister.”
A spokesman for HSE said: “Concerns have been raised with HSE and these are being looked into. We remain in contact with HS2 in order to review any plans that would affect workers, protesters or rescue personnel.”
The Metropolitan Police did not wish to comment.
A spokeswoman for HS2 said: “We have had police and paramedics on the site and have had the London fire brigade there to assess the operation, and safety of all . . . remains at the forefront of everything we are doing.”
Defiant daughter
As her father feared for her life at his home in the Hebrides Blue Sandford said she had no regrets about joining the London tunnel protest (Moira Kerr writes).
Speaking from the heart of the tunnel in a late-night call on Saturday, the 18-year-old said: “I’m prepared to stay as long as it takes, I don’t regret doing this, I think it has a real chance of stopping HS2.”
She added: “We’re all doing well, there’s a lot of jokes and we’re staying strong. There’s a lot of water dripping down — most of the sleeping bags are wet and my clothes are soaked, but we’re safe.”
She claimed: “The bailiffs are being unsafe in jumping down on top of us in the down shaft and dropping loads of dirt on us . . . and removing our drainage system from the park, which is causing a lot of water to drip down, which caused the collapses before.
“The tunnel is completely stable now, we have not had any more collapses but as a precautionary measure it will be much safer once the bailiffs put back the drainage system and start working safely.”
The pupil, who is on school strike over government inaction on climate change, also claimed that the bailiffs were refusing to send an oxygen monitor down to the end of the tunnel.

image.caption: Roc Sandford said he was proud of Blue, right, and Lazer, with sister Savannah

author: Moira Kerr

https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.title: Climate activists spread the digging as new tunnel found in north London
https://www.thetimes.com/article/climate.text:
A copycat tunnel has been dug and occupied by climate activists who are trying to stop trees being felled to make way for flats in north London.
Bailiffs for Islington council found the underground chamber beneath Dixon Clark Court on Highbury Corner, where a camp nicknamed “little forest” was built to protect seven mature trees.
The tunnel is two miles from the one dug secretly near Euston station by a group — including the veteran activist known as Swampy — that opposes the construction of the HS2 high-speed rail link.
The discovery comes after Swampy, whose real name is Daniel Hooper, 48, told The Times that the authorities should expect more underground battles with environmental activists because more tunnels were planned.
Activists at the Highbury Corner camp said bailiffs found the new tunnel at 5am yesterday. The tunnellers had used similar methods to those deployed at Euston. A spokesman for the group said there were a number of protesters inside. The Times understands one is Maria Gallastegui, who last month was removed from England’s Tree of the Year, in Hackney, east London, moments before it was felled.
Analysing photographs of the new dig, Peter Faulding, a rescue specialist who removed Hooper from a protest tunnel in 1996, said that the activists appeared to have constructed “a living area at the end of the tunnel”.
He added: “The area . . . appears to be a bell chamber for living in. Without shoring, this area is very unstable and could collapse at any time.”
Protesters have been taking shifts living at the site for almost four months to try to save the trees, which were due to be felled to make way for a six-storey block of 14 private flats, which Islington council says will fund 25 council flats.
The tunnel is understood to be much smaller that its Euston counterpart, which at 100ft long and 15ft deep has prevented bailiffs evicting six protesters for 11 days so far.
“It is in an area of major traffic congestion and air pollution, in the most densely populated London borough with the least green space per head outside of the City,” the spokesman said.
Gallastegui, 62, said: “Our governments, local and national, are . . . not representing the people. They declare a climate and environment emergency and then carry on destroying trees and countryside. It’s got to stop.”
Diarmaid Ward, executive member for housing and development at Islington council, said the new development would result in 25 “desperately needed” council homes. He said: “At the same time, the project will deliver 63 new trees, an extra 100sq m of communal garden space for residents and a number of plantings and landscaping improvements designed to improve biodiversity and address air quality issues.
“The council has done everything we can to avoid legal and enforcement action and had reached an agreement with XR [Extinction Rebellion], the initial group of protesters, that they would leave the site voluntarily and the council would use the money we would have spent on legal fees on even more trees, in addition to the 63 we had already planned to replace the six being felled.
“It’s truly disheartening that people who claim to care about both trees and homes have forced an outcome resulting in fewer trees for the borough, significant costs, and further delays to building much-needed council homes for local families in desperate need.”

image.caption: Maria Gallastegui occupies a chamber at Highbury Corner, two miles from the HS2 protest at Euston

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/lord.title: Lord Fraser of Corriegarth obituary
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/lord.subtitle: Former Conservative Party treasurer and Barings banker who famously confronted Extinction Rebellion in his dressing gown
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/lord.text:
It was one of the defining pictures of the Extinction Rebellion protests in October 2019: Lord Fraser of Corriegarth, a Tory donor and former party treasurer, emerging from his home in the heart of Westminster clad in nothing more than a white dressing gown and monogrammed slippers to confront a colourful band of noisy protesters whose carnival had turned from Smith Square into Lord North Street.
Jack Hill, the Times photographer who caught the occasion, recalled: “It is a beautiful street and I ran ahead to capture the contradiction of the protest band and the genteel surroundings. I noticed a man at his front door in his dressing gown and slippers. He saw the band and started waving his fist angrily at them. Was he really doing that?”
The marchers had spent the previous night camped on nearby Millbank, where the combination of banging drums and police helicopters was likely to have disturbed Fraser’s sleep. “As the band approached, his frustration overcame him and he walked out into the street to confront them and started shaking his fist again and then followed that up with the double handed ‘come on’ gesture more commonly seen on football terraces,” recalled Hill.
It was a rare public gesture by Fraser, a former Barings banker, proud Scot and staunch unionist. During the Scottish independence referendum of 2014 he made donations totalling £200,000 to the Better Together campaign. Under David Cameron’s leadership he gave more than £2.5 million to the Tories, while a further £10,000 made its way from his deep pockets into Theresa May’s 2017 general election campaign.
Alexander Andrew Macdonell Fraser was born in Edinburgh in 1946, the only child of Walter Fraser, QC, a judge who was later ennobled as Lord Fraser of Tullybelton, and his wife Cynthia (née Macdonell). He was educated at Aysgarth prep school, North Yorkshire, and at Eton, where he was a strong oarsman.
He read politics, philosophy and economics at St John’s College, Oxford, before joining the City. In 1982 he married Sarah Jones, a silversmith based in the City of London. That was dissolved in 1985 and he is survived by their son, Henry, known as Bertie, a property developer. In 2010 he married Rebecca Ramsay (née Shaw-Mackenzie), who also survives him with four stepchildren, Catriona, Irene, Euan and Ruaridh; his eldest stepson, Douglas, died in Cambodia in 2012.
Fraser had joined Baring Securities in 1984 and was head of equities when the bank collapsed in 1995 after Nick Leeson, a rogue trader, ran up losses of £827 million. It later emerged that three years before the collapse Fraser had been one of the recipients of a fax from the head of Barings’ operations in Singapore expressing concern at the extent of Leeson’s power.
In 1987 he acquired the Corriegarth Estate, at the southern end of Loch Ness, where he was a generous host to friends during the shooting season. He made donations to the Sea Cadets, St John’s College and Eton. Sir Eric Anderson, the head master (obituary, April 23, 2020), recalled at his retirement in 2009 how he enjoyed opening letters like the one he had received from Fraser the previous year that read: “I’m sorry for you having to raise money for Eton. I hope the attached may help a little.” Clipped on the back was a cheque for £1 million.
Fraser was well connected throughout the Far East and, having done well in the City, sometimes invested in his own right. In the mid-1990s he put $250,000 into an emerging property company in Beijing. Twelve years later Soho China was valued at $1.9 billion when it was floated on the Hong Kong stock exchange, making $100 million for Fraser. No longer needing to work, he settled in London, becoming influential in the Conservative Party and in 2015 he was appointed party treasurer. The following year he was one of 46 former aides, advisers and ministers to feature in Cameron’s resignation honours list.
Fraser, who stood 6ft 2in tall and was good looking with a shock of white hair, would have retained his low profile had it not been for the Extinction Rebellion confrontation in Lord North Street 16 months ago. Observers hoped that beneath his robe he was wearing shorts of some description because, as the Times journalist Helen Rumbelow observed at the time, the belt on his dressing gown looked worryingly insecure.
Lord Fraser of Corriegarth, Conservative Party treasurer, 2015-16, was born on December 2, 1946. He died of a brain tumour on February 6, 2021, aged 74

image.caption: Fraser would have kept his low profile were it not for the Lord North Street set-to

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.title: Hard left and foreign activists try to topple Britain’s statues
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/politics/art.text:
Anti-capitalist academics, hard-left groups and foreign activists are accused of fuelling campaigns to remove statues across the country despite public opposition, The Times can reveal.
The groups include the Socialist Workers Party and a member of the new diversity commission set up by Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London.
The opposing campaign group Save Our Statues fears the erasing of history after the killing of George Floyd, which prompted global protests last summer by movements such as Black Lives Matter.
More than a dozen schools and universities have changed their names or renamed buildings in the wake of the antiracist protests.
A monument to Sir Robert Geffrye, a slave trader, outside the Museum of the Home, in Hackney, east London, is under threat after protests by Stand Up To Racism Hackney — which has 222 followers on Twitter. The museum consulted the public after the Black Lives Matter protests and decided to keep it. It is to review that decision after the statue’s hands were daubed with red paint.
Protesters include Sasha Simic, who is also a member of the Socialist Workers Party and wrote on Twitter: “I want to piss on the ashes of capitalism” and “Capitalism has no ‘magic’. It is theft. We will bring the thieves to justice one day.” Simic could not be reached for comment.
The statue of Geffrye acknowledges his donation to build almshouses. A survey found 71 per cent of people were in favour of removing it, but people who were friends of the museum, donors or volunteers voted 61 per cent in favour of keeping it.
Toyin Agbetu, who was this week announced as a member of Khan’s racism commission, featured in a video of a protest at the museum posted on Momentum Hackney’s Facebook group with a megaphone exclaiming, “The passage of time, doesn’t wipe out the crime” and “Geffrye must fall”.
Agbetu, who once confronted the Queen at Westminster Abbey during a service to mark the abolition of slavery, made a video raising scepticism about the Pfizer coronavirus vaccine in November, before it was approved. He posted it alongside a message that read: “Apparently a magical vaccine is around the corner from the Viagra specialists. There’s a lot of nonsense out there and it’s coming from the clowns in No 10.”
In the video, recorded in November, he said: “As a scientific breakthrough yes it looks promising but using it now, when there are so many questions unanswered because of a ‘profit over people’ government that wants to privatise speed over safety and effectiveness is ethically unsound.
“If ministers and their human shields want to give it to their mums that’s up to them. But let’s see politicians do a John Gummer, take it live on TV with their grandparents and allow us to monitor them for nine months Big Brother style first, before telling us they’re going to roll it out en masse.”
Khan’s office said: “All panel members were assessed for the role by a review panel and a decision made based on what they could bring to the role. Toyin Agbetu was appointed for his significant expertise, knowledge and experience as a social rights activist and in setting up Ligali, which challenges the misrepresentation of African people and culture in the media. His vast experience will provide a valuable contribution to the commission.”
Agbetu told The Times: “My position on this important matter is not to dismiss the legitimate concerns of people who were let down by the government who denied ethnic disproportionality was a factor leading to unnecessary deaths in our community during the pandemic. Vaccines are an important part of the solution to help resolve the global crises we all face due to coronavirus.”
There are 130 Labour-led councils reviewing statues and road names.
A veteran Socialist Workers Party member has spoken out in support of removal of a statue of the Scouts founder Robert Baden-Powell. Weyman Bennett went on LBC radio to call for the removal of the statue in Poole Harbour, Dorset. He said: “He was obviously involved in the murder of black people in South Africa in terms of shooting people . . . that had surrendered. We should put statues up to genuine people that made progress for humanity.”
Bennett told The Times: “In a series of wars in Africa he showed contempt for black people. This is hardly someone who should be remembered as an example to remember and follow.”
This week Boris Johnson ordered a review into the extreme fringes of the hard left and far right in the UK hijacking movements including Black Lives Matter and Extinction Rebellion.
In Piccadilly Gardens, Manchester, a statue of Sir Robert Peel, the former prime minister and founder of the Metropolitan Police is under threat after a petition by Sami Pinarbasi, a left-wing academic at Manchester Metropolitan University. Pinarbasi told The Times: “I started my campaign because I want a better future for my country.”
The Times has found a YouTube video where he says: “Capitalism creates and weaponises racial bias. It goes hand in glove with racism, just as it uses sexism, homophobia, disablism, ageism . . . The holding facilities and the hostile environment and other presentations of the virulent racist bastions of Toryism represented in the 21st century.”
In Carmarthen, south Wales, Save our Statues said it found that a petition against an obelisk to Thomas Picton, who is said to have executed slaves, was hijacked by foreigners. On a petition with 18,646 signatures only 3,897 of the responders were based in the UK. The majority (10,845) were from the US, while responses also came from Australia, Greenland, Tonga and Tuvalu. In a council survey more than two thirds of those responding — 1,613 of people compared to 744 — urged it not to do anything about the memorial to Picton.
The council decided to press ahead with putting up a plaque to explain Picton’s connection to slavery.
Last autumn the City of London Corporation ran a consultation in which 71 per cent of the public said “items of contested heritage” should remain where they are. However, last month it announced its intention to purge from its grade I listed Guildhall a renowned statue of Sir John Cass by Louis-François Roubiliac, considered the finest sculptor working in 18th-century Britain.
Richard Bingley, general secretary of Save Our Statues, said that due diligence needed to be carried out on the people behind these campaigns. He said: “During the past year we have witnessed an unprecedented array of attacks and vandalism upon our precious physical heritage in the UK, seemingly with no due diligence whatsoever.”
Research by The Times showed that six schools had been renamed and eight others changed the title of buildings such as halls and houses. Statues have been removed from two schools in England.
Names deemed problematic have not been limited to those connected to slavery. A school in East Sussex is renaming a house honouring JK Rowling after pupils questioned whether she “represented the school’s core values” due to comments she made about transgender issues. In a letter also calling for a house named after Winston Churchill to be changed, pupils at Seaford Head School wrote that they did not want to “promote anyone or anything” that encouraged “intolerance and discrimination”.
Haberdashers’ Adams, a grammar school in Newport, Shropshire, renamed a house that had been named after Robert Clive, the first governor of Bengal, who is credited with laying the foundations of the British empire in India.
Governors of Beckford Primary School in northwest London agreed to change its name, which it took from William Beckford, an 18th-century slave owner. However, a suggestion to name it after Beryl Gilroy, head for 14 years from 1968 and one of the country’s first black head teachers, was voted against by pupils and parents. It will instead become West Hampstead Primary School.
City University has declared that the Cass Business School will be renamed. However, more than 3,500 people signed a petition saying their degrees will be devalued if the school drops the name of Sir John Cass, who was linked to the slave trade.
Richard Bingley, of Save Our Statues, said that due diligence needed to be carried out on the people behind campaigns. He claimed: “It is patently obvious that many of these attacks and protests have been incited by foreign groups and fringe movements.”

https://www.thetimes.com/sport/athletics.title: Ping-pong prodigy Anna Hursey is batting for Joe Biden
https://www.thetimes.com/sport/athletics.text:
Anna Hursey was ten years old when she made her international debut on the professional table tennis circuit. A year later the Welsh prodigy became the youngest athlete to compete in the Commonwealth Games.
Alongside her fierce competitive streak, which has seen off adult opponents, runs a passion to tackle the climate change crisis, which caught her attention when she began watching the news.
And now, still aged only 14, she has been spotted by President Biden, who has asked for her help in making his climate initiative a success.
The US embassy sent her a message last week inquiring if she would help the president to tackle what it said was the “most urgent priority” of his administration. Anna was asked to speak to the embassy about working with it to promote the message to young people.
“I never thought something like this would happen to me,” she told The Times. “I was really surprised but I was excited to talk to them about it.”
Anna is scheduled to speak to Yael Lempert, the interim head of the US embassy in London, about how, in the run-up to the summit Biden is hosting on Earth Day, April 22, she can help spread messages about combating climate change and reducing carbon emissions.
“I am a bit nervous,” she said. “I wrote down some sentences I can say to her and I have been doing a lot more research on climate change.”
At the Commonwealth Games on the Gold Coast in Australia in 2018 Anna won her opening game before finally being knocked out in the quarter-finals of the women’s team competition. She is ranked No 1 in Wales for under-15s and No 2 among the seniors.
Last year the United Nations made her the “young champion” of its Sports for Climate Action Framework.
More than 110 sports teams and organisations have signed the framework, agreeing to promote greater environmental responsibility.
The 2015 Paris agreement, which America rejoined last month, aims to limit global warming to less than 2C above pre-industrial levels. Britain is a signatory.
Anna, who has a British father and a Chinese mother, is a rising star in her sport, and organisations appear eager to use her to spread their messages.
As an asthma-sufferer, she says she feels the effects of air pollution more than others, but as an athlete competing at international level, she is aware how hard it is to live a carbon-neutral lifestyle.
“I do travel but I always offset all the carbon,” she said. “I work out how many miles I go by car and on the plane and I put that into carbonfootprint.com and it tells us how much money to invest in different projects.
“Saving energy, recycling, using less fossil fuels, walking, cycling instead of driving when possible — there is so much we can do. Small, large, every change and effort is important. I want to be involved, working with others towards the answers.”
Born in Carmarthen, west Wales, Anna was spotted for her table tennis talent at a young age, and since six she has attended intensive training camps in China, where she would practise up to seven hours a day.
She made her international senior debut aged ten and in 2019 relocated to China permanently to train with the best in the city of Harbin, in the northeastern province of Heilongjiang.
When the coronavirus pandemic broke out, she returned to Britain, and she now lives and trains in Cardiff at the national sports centre with the Welsh senior squad.
While training with the aim to win medals at the Birmingham 2022 Commonwealth Games and the Paris 2024 Summer Olympics, she is still having to do her school work.
A pupil at Inter High, an online secondary school, she has been doing web video classes since before the pandemic as a way to fit her lessons around her training schedule.
After speaking to The Times yesterday afternoon she had a maths lesson and geography lesson to attend before putting in more hours of training.
“Table tennis hasn’t been the most popular sport in the UK but it’s definitely getting more popular, and in China it’s been the biggest sport for years,” she said.
“I just want to try to use my voice to let people know about climate change, and hopefully they can take some action in their own lives to help.”
The British GretasGreta Thunberg, the Swedish teenager, has energised the climate debate and mobilised youngsters to speak out. British campaigners are finding their own Gretas who are passionate, eloquent and determined to effect change.
Elizabeth Fiennes, 14, daughter of the explorer Sir Ranulph Fiennes, addressed an event in parliament last year saying: “Your generation is responsible, and those before you. My generation is begging you to stop.”
Elsie Luna, 12, a former chess champion, has been promoted by Extinction Rebellion as “the UK’s answer to Greta” and lobbied oil companies at their London offices, asking to speak to executives about the need to stop using fossil fuels.
Bella Ramsey, 17, an actress in Game of Thrones, spoke at a Greenpeace event to launch a film highlighting the threat to turtles from climate change, pollution and overfishing.
Bella Lack, 18, is an “ambassador” for the Born Free Foundation, RSPCA and Jane Goodall Institute and has spoken at events attended by world leaders, including one on the illegal wildlife trade hosted by the Duke of Cambridge.

image.caption: Anna Hursey, who is ranked No 1 in Wales for under-15s, says she is “a bit nervous” after the US embassy asked her to help President Biden’s climate change initiative

https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/hs2-.title: HS2 protests: father of Euston tunnellers has strong views on parenting
https://www.thetimes.com/uk/article/hs2-.text:
To lose one child in an underground network could be regarded as misfortune — to lose two looks a little careless. Yet Roc Sandford, 62, does not appear surprised. The father of 18-year-old Blue, who is occupying 100ft of tunnels beneath Euston Square Gardens in central London in protest against HS2 after her brother Lazer, 20, left the site last night and was arrested by police, smiles mysteriously when asked at what point he discovered his children’s plans: “I’d rather not say.”
Before Lazer’s exit the siblings had been down there for two weeks already, as the HS2 contractors attempted to evict them without risking lives. Sandford has been in contact with his children. They have been able to text him because there is mobile phone reception at the bottom of the one of the down-shafts but their batteries were running low. Bailiffs spent 25 hours cutting a steel pipe to which Lazer had chained himself only for him to escape deeper into the tunnels on Friday evening, but last night he finally gave himself up. The situation has made Sandford very anxious. “It’s one of the worst times of my life. I’ve been terrified that they’re going to get seriously hurt or killed,” he adds.
This doesn’t mean that he disapproves of their antics. Sandford is a long-term environmental campaigner. Three of his four children are activists. Each has been through “a rite of passage of sorts”, he says. For his oldest daughter, Savannah, 22, that was April Fool’s Day 2019, when she stripped in the public gallery of the House of Commons during a Brexit debate.
The same year his son, Lazer, glued himself to the Brazilian embassy in protest against deforestation. Blue has already been arrested for attaching herself to Nelson’s Column and has published a handbook for young environmentalists. But the tunnel, Sandford thinks, is her defining moment. “It is something completely different and quite amazing,” he says.
At this rate, I suggest the most shocking thing would be if one of his children became an accountant. “If they wanted to I’d be right behind them,” he says happily. Sandford has strong views about raising children: “I think I’m probably quite a strict parent, where I feel strictness is needed,” he says. But he is a big believer in the importance of ideals. His other child, Cato, 31, is a physicist working in renewable energy, so even he has not strayed far from the family path.
Sandford is speaking to me from a shed on Gometra, the Scottish island he has owned since the Nineties. It was on this island in the Inner Hebrides where the family’s environmental conversion took place. Soon after he bought it, he became embroiled in a long-running battle with salmon farmers intent on setting up in the surrounding waters. As well as the sea lice that proliferate in salmon enclosures, campaigners say underwater alarms intended to frighten seals also affect whales and porpoises. “It’s seriously damaging to them. And unlawful, because you’re supposed to get licences to disturb cetaceans. I don’t want to bore you ...” he says, trailing off.
He succeeded in seeing them off four times only to fail on the fifth. It was this he thinks that made the children — Blue in particular — take an interest in environmental issues. “She saw us fighting really hard and saw us failing. I think she began to realise that you can’t necessarily succeed even if you’re on the right side.”
The children had plenty of time to become used to an alternative lifestyle. When Sandford moved in, the island had been deserted since the 19th century. At first he imported diesel to power the generator. Then he installed a wind turbine, which failed, and a solar panel, which blew away. He no longer uses heating, lighting the fire only a few nights a week in the depths of winter, and washes his clothes in a bucket. He has stopped taking flights and given up his car, his camper van and his quad bike. Now he is experimenting with “low-carbon cooking”: par-boiling food before putting it into a container and allowing it to steam.
Not all of his experiments in environmentalism have worked. “I gave up shampoo and soap and things, and that was all fine. Then I gave up toothpaste and it didn’t work, so I’ve taken toothpaste up again.” He has also tried to create what he has described as a “utopia”; anyone can come and live on the island rent-free. How many houses are there? “How many legally habitable houses?” he asks. “Probably zero.” It would be more accurate to describe them as “ruins”, he suggests.
The island has no doctor or school. It is “beyond the reach of the welfare state”, he says. All his children, from two separate relationships, went to private schools in London, where their mothers live. Sandford also spends some of the year in the capital. He travels back and forth to Gometra by train, boat and bike, a journey that takes between 12 hours and two days. The most peculiar aspect of all this — in what is, let’s face it, stiff competition — is that despite being a committed vegan, Sandford farms sheep. He sees himself as “a custodian” of the flock, he says. His one regret is that the animals are not slaughtered on Gometra but transported to the mainland and sold: “I’m always grappling with that.”
The farm provides an income. Could he survive without it? “I wouldn’t be destitute in any way. I’m extremely lucky.” Sandford’s family, it should be said, is not short of funds. Both his parents came from “upper-class” families, but his father, an Eton-educated publisher, rebelled: “He wanted to challenge the system.” So he turned the family home, Hatfield Court, a 40-room mansion in Herefordshire, into an open house for waifs and strays. Roc, who was named after “the patron saint of mad dogs, sea storms and the falsely accused” grew up in the mayhem. “I’d come back and there’d be someone sleeping in my bedroom,” he recalls.
His own activism gained a new focus in 2018 when he saw a tweet from a man called Roger Hallam saying: “I’m going to sit down in front of the traffic in Marble Arch.” Sandford, who was in his London home, cycled over and joined him in an effort “to stop business as usual and make people understand that the world was on fire”. The experience was uncomfortable: he was getting in the way and people were angry. “I found it very painful. But I was conscious that I’d found the way in to stopping this if it could be done.”
It was the genesis of Extinction Rebellion, whose ethos Sandford’s children have embraced along with his lifestyle. It is hard to make out exactly what he thinks of this. On Friday, as efforts to remove the protesters from the tunnel intensified. The protesters have no means of raising the alarm if something goes wrong. As a result, Sandford is not getting much sleep.
I ask if he regrets setting them on this path. “I do wonder if I should have lied to them about the climate emergency,” he says. “But I’ve always wanted there to be honesty between us.” If the children think a risk is worth taking, “I stand behind them all the way”.
